ar_2_swing_station.blurb: Swing Station is the steep wall at Fitzgerald Mountain, in the Fayetteville and Springdale corner of northwest Arkansas. All 25 climbs are bolted sport lines, roughly 35 to 50 feet tall, on sandstone that runs from fair to excellent, with a few holds still working loose. Grades begin around 5.10 and reach into 5.12, with most of the weight in the 5.11 and low 5.12 range. That makes it a pumpy, overhanging crag for climbers past the beginner stage rather than a first outdoor day. Many lines have fixed draws, and the lower-offs are simple hooks. A helmet and a stick clip are worth bringing. Sun exposure is not well documented.

ar_invasion_wall.blurb: Invasion Wall is a steep sport crag in the Cowell area of Newton County, in the Arkansas Ozarks, at around 1,970 feet. About two dozen bolted lines work up a cliffline of stacked roofs, so the climbing is overhanging and powerful, and the roofs let it stay climbable in wet weather. The grades are concentrated at the hard end: nearly every route falls in the 5.12 and 5.13 range, with only a couple of easier lines near 5.10 and 5.11, plus one very hard boulder problem at the start of the cliff. This is a destination for strong sport climbers rather than beginners. The cliffline is visible as soon as you reach its base.

ar_walls_of_moria.blurb: Walls of Moria is a sandstone wall on the West Side of Horseshoe Canyon Ranch, in Newton County near the Buffalo National River in Arkansas. It holds about two dozen climbs, a blend of bolted sport lines and trad cracks. The grades are friendly: most land between 5.7 and 5.10, with a handful of 5.11s and a single 5.12, so it suits climbers building up through the moderate grades. The wall is lower angle than much of the ranch, with sloping holds and runnels of water running between lines, and it can stay damp after rain. The ranch as a whole is known for good sandstone and a campground close to the cliffs.

ar_heaven_boulders.blurb: Heaven Boulders is a small cluster of boulders and a short bluff in the Richland Creek area of north-central Arkansas, in a quiet wooded setting. The two dozen problems span roughly V2 to V9, with a fair number in the middle grades and several hard ones at the top end. Expect compression lines, roofs, cracks and pinches, and big boulders whose overhangs form small alcoves. Holds are plentiful on both the boulders and the bluff, which is where the name comes from. The boulders sit only a short walk from the road, so a visit works as a quick stop rather than a full day trip. Sun and shade have not been described well.
ar_heaven_boulders.approach: A short walk of about 100 meters south of the road from the pull-off; an obvious trail leaves the road just up from the parking spot.
